opus-5.5.text:
I think when we look back, the skepticism will seem pretty natural, honestly. People have been promised humanoid robots for decades, and for most of that time the demos were impressive but the deployments never came. So I don't hold it against anyone who looked at a company like Foundation and said, "Prove it."

What I expect people will notice in hindsight is that the hard part was never just building one robot that can do something cool on a stage. The hard part is manufacturing, reliability, safety, servicing, and getting a customer to trust a machine enough to put it into a real workflow and keep it there. That's where we've spent a lot of our energy: on the boring parts that make scale possible, not just the flashy parts that make a good video.

So my hope is that the story people tell later is less "they had a breakthrough moment" and more "they kept showing up." Robots going into real facilities, doing real hours, getting better with every deployment, and the units coming off the line faster each quarter. Scale doesn't arrive all at once; it compounds. At some point the conversation shifts from "Can they actually do this?" to "Why didn't we see this coming?"

And frankly, a little skepticism is healthy. It keeps us honest. We'd rather be measured by what's working in the field than by what we say on a podcast, so the best answer I can give is: watch the deployments. That's where the argument gets settled.

r001.rationale: The response predicts scaling deployments and increasing production, but it does not state or clearly imply that Foundation will reach 10,000 deployed robots.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I'll look back on it as completely reasonable, honestly. Skepticism is the right default when someone tells you they're going to put humanoid robots into real factories and real workplaces at scale. The history of robotics is littered with incredible demos that never turned into products, so if people weren't skeptical, I'd be a little worried about them.

What I hope I'll be able to say, looking back, is that we earned the credibility rather than asked for it. The way you answer skepticism isn't with a better video, it's with units in the field doing useful work, day after day, with customers who are paying for that work and coming back for more. That's a very different bar than "can the robot walk across a stage," and it's the one we've tried to hold ourselves to.

And I think the thing skeptics underestimate isn't the hardware, it's the pace of learning. Every robot we deploy is a data source, and the systems get better in ways that compound. So the gap between "this is a cool prototype" and "this is doing a shift" closes faster than people's intuition says it should. Five years from now I suspect the question won't be whether it was possible, it'll be why it took everyone so long to believe it.

But I'll also say, some of the skepticism will have been right about specifics. We'll have gotten timelines wrong, we'll have hit problems we didn't anticipate. That's fine. Being right about the direction and wrong about the exact dates is how most big technology shifts go.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses deploying robots at scale but does not predict that Foundation will reach 10,000 deployed robots.

astra-6.text: I think we’ll look back and say the skepticism was understandable. Building a robot is one thing; deploying a fleet that does useful work reliably every day is a very different challenge. We have to prove we can do that. My hope is that, over time, the conversation shifts from “Can you deploy these at scale?” to “Where do we need them next?” But you earn that shift through deployments and results.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proving reliable fleet deployment at scale but does not predict Foundation will reach 10,000 deployed robots.

sol-6.1.text: I think we’ll look back and understand why people were skeptical. Robots have been promised for a long time, and there’s a big difference between showing a demo and putting a machine to work reliably every day. For us, the answer has to be deployment: robots doing useful work, customers seeing value, and then doing that again and again at greater scale. If we execute, I think what feels unlikely today will start to feel pretty obvious in hindsight.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling deployments generally but does not predict that Foundation will reach 10,000 deployed robots.
